title: Ἡ λιθίνη ναῦς
titleEn: The Ship Turned to Stone — Odyssey 13.113–216
source: Homer, The Odyssey, Greek text of A. T. Murray (Loeb Classical Library; London: Heinemann, New York: Putnam, 1919), public domain; TEI from PerseusDL/canonical-greekLit tlg0012.tlg002.perseus-grc2, sha256 7d7ffafb6c51f8c2. Text as printed: Murray sets no quotation marks round speeches, and none are added. Pronunciation: reconstructed Attic, after W. S. Allen, Vox Graeca — an admitted convention; Homer's own pronunciation was older and is not recoverable in detail. Romanization: standard classical transliteration (ē/ō; th/ph/ch; y for υ, u in diphthongs; h = rough breathing; ēi/āi/ōi for iota subscript; ï for a separately sounded ι; accents omitted). Scansion: made by program from the text and checked; it shows one defensible reading of each line, and the notes say where a line is irregular. All translations were made fresh from the Greek for Lectorium.
about: The Phaeacian ship runs into the harbour and the crew lay the sleeping Odysseus on the sand, with his gifts set down beside an olive tree off the road, and go home. Poseidon, who has not forgotten his threats, complains to Zeus that mortals of his own stock slight him. Zeus tells him to do as he likes, and when Poseidon proposes to smash the returning ship and cover the Phaeacians’ city with a mountain, Zeus advises him to turn the ship into a stone within sight of the whole city, keeping the mountain in the plan. Poseidon goes to Scheria and turns the ship to stone as she comes in, and Alcinous, seeing it, recalls the old prophecy and bids the Phaeacians stop giving escorts and sacrifice twelve bulls, which they set about doing. Odysseus wakes in his own land without knowing it, for Athena has veiled it in mist, and he laments, blaming the Phaeacians for not keeping their word to bring him to Ithaca, and resolves to count his goods.

sentences.t: ἔνθ’ οἵ γ’ εἰσέλασαν, πρὶν εἰδότες·
sentences.tr: enth’ hoi g’ eiselasan, prin eidotes·
sentences.l: There they drove in, knowing beforehand;
sentences.i: There they drove the ship in, already knowing the place;
sentences.n: ἔνθα ‘there’ looks back to the harbour and cave described at the end of the last part, and the subject οἵ γ’ ‘they’ is the Phaeacian crew (the old demonstrative serving as a pronoun). εἰσέλασαν is the aorist of εἰσελαύνω ‘drive in’, said of a ship urged on by oars. πρίν is here an adverb ‘before, earlier’ and εἰδότες is the perfect participle of οἶδα ‘knowing’; the Greek gives it no object, and the sense is that they knew the place already. The unit ends at the ano teleia in the middle of line 113.

sentences.t:
ἡ μὲν ἔπειτα
ἠπείρῳ ἐπέκελσεν, ὅσον τ’ ἐπὶ ἥμισυ πάσης,
σπερχομένη·
sentences.tr:
hē men epeita
ēpeirōi epekelsen, hoson t’ epi hēmisy pasēs,
sperchomenē·
sentences.i: and the ship then ran aground on the mainland, as far as half her whole length, in her haste;
sentences.n: ἡ μέν is ‘she’, the ship (the article as a pronoun), set against οἱ δέ ‘and they’ in line 116, the men. ἠπείρῳ is the dative of ἤπειρος ‘mainland’, and ἐπέκελσεν the aorist of ἐπικέλλω ‘run a ship ashore’. ὅσον τ’ ἐπὶ ἥμισυ πάσης is ‘as far as up to half of the whole’; πάσης is feminine and agrees with an understood νηός, and ‘length’ is supplied by the sense. σπερχομένη, from σπέρχω ‘hasten, press on’, is a present participle agreeing with ἡ: she was in haste. The unit begins and ends mid-line.

sentences.t: τοῖον γὰρ ἐπείγετο χέρσ’ ἐρετάων·
sentences.tr: toion gar epeigeto chers’ eretaōn·
sentences.l: for so was she urged on by the hands of the rowers;
sentences.i: for the hands of the rowers drove her on so hard;
sentences.n: τοῖον is an adverbial accusative, ‘to such a degree’, and γάρ gives the reason for σπερχομένη: she ran up so far because she was driven so hard. ἐπείγετο is the imperfect passive of ἐπείγω ‘press on, urge’. χέρσ’ is read as an elided χέρσι, the dative plural of χείρ ‘hand’ (‘by the hands’), with the genitive ἐρετάων ‘of the rowers’, the Homeric ending -άων for Attic -ῶν; ἐρέτης ‘rower’ belongs with ἐρετμόν ‘oar’.

sentences.t:
οἱ δ’ ἐκ νηὸς βάντες ἐϋζύγου ἤπειρόνδε
πρῶτον Ὀδυσσῆα γλαφυρῆς ἐκ νηὸς ἄειραν
αὐτῷ σύν τε λίνῳ καὶ ῥήγεϊ σιγαλόεντι,
κὰδ δ’ ἄρ’ ἐπὶ ψαμάθῳ ἔθεσαν δεδμημένον ὕπνῳ,
sentences.tr:
hoi d’ ek nēos bantes eÿzygou ēpeironde
prōton Odyssēa glaphyrēs ek nēos aeiran
autōi syn te linōi kai rhēgeï sigaloenti,
kad d’ ar’ epi psamathōi ethesan dedmēmenon hypnōi,
sentences.l:
And they, out of the ship stepping, the well-yoked, onto the mainland,
first Odysseus out of the hollow ship lifted,
himself together with both the linen cloth and the rug glossy,
and down on the sand set him, overcome by sleep,
sentences.i: They stepped out of the well-yoked ship onto the mainland and first lifted Odysseus out of the hollow ship, just as he was, together with the linen cloth and the glossy rug, and set him down on the sand, overcome by sleep,
sentences.n: The subject is again the crew, οἱ δέ ‘and they’, now ashore; Odysseus is still asleep and is carried out first. ἐϋζύγου is the epithet of a ship, ‘well-yoked’; ζυγόν is ‘yoke’ and also a ship’s cross-bench, and the exact sense of the compound is not certain. βάντες is the aorist participle of βαίνω, and the -δε of ἤπειρόνδε marks the goal, ‘to the mainland’. ἄειραν is the aorist of ἀείρω ‘lift’. αὐτῷ σύν τε λίνῳ καὶ ῥήγεϊ is ‘himself together with both linen and rug’: the datives follow σύν, and ῥῆγος is a rug or blanket (the ῥῆγος and linen cloth that were spread for him on the ship at line 73). σιγαλόεντι is ‘glossy’, the traditional gloss. In κὰδ … ἔθεσαν, tmesis for κατέθεσαν, the preverb κατά is written κὰδ before δ’. ψαμάθῳ is the dative of ψάμαθος ‘sand’, and δεδμημένον, the perfect passive participle of δαμάζω ‘overpower’, agrees with Ὀδυσσῆα. The unit stops at a comma because the sentence runs to line 121.

sentences.t:
ἐκ δὲ κτήματ’ ἄειραν, ἅ οἱ Φαίηκες ἀγαυοὶ
ὤπασαν οἴκαδ’ ἰόντι διὰ μεγάθυμον Ἀθήνην.
sentences.tr:
ek de ktēmat’ aeiran, ha hoi Phaiēkes agauoi
ōpasan oikad’ ionti dia megathymon Athēnēn.
sentences.l:
and out the goods they lifted, which to him the noble Phaeacians
gave as he went homeward, on account of great-hearted Athena.
sentences.i: Then they lifted out the goods that the noble Phaeacians had given him as he went homeward, thanks to great-hearted Athena.
sentences.n: ἐκ … ἄειραν is tmesis, the preverb ἐκ standing apart from the verb: ‘lifted out’, the same verb as in line 117, now with κτήματα ‘possessions, goods’ as object. The relative ἅ is neuter plural, and οἱ ‘to him’ is the dative of the receiver. ὤπασαν is the aorist of ὀπάζω ‘bestow’, and ἰόντι the dative participle of εἶμι ‘go’, agreeing with οἱ: ‘to him as he went’. ἀγαυοί is ‘noble’, the house rendering. διά with the accusative gives the cause, ‘because of’, and μεγάθυμον ‘great-hearted’ qualifies Ἀθήνην. It continues the sentence of the last unit, after the comma at the end of line 119.

sentences.t:
καὶ τὰ μὲν οὖν παρὰ πυθμέν’ ἐλαίης ἀθρόα θῆκαν
ἐκτὸς ὁδοῦ, μή πώς τις ὁδιτάων ἀνθρώπων,
πρίν γ’ Ὀδυσῆ’ ἔγρεσθαι, ἐπελθὼν δηλήσαιτο·
sentences.tr:
kai ta men oun para pythmen’ elaiēs athroa thēkan
ektos hodou, mē pōs tis hoditaōn anthrōpōn,
prin g’ Odysē’ egresthai, epelthōn dēlēsaito·
sentences.i: So they put the goods down together in a heap beside the trunk of the olive, out of the road, in case some passing traveller should come upon them and do them harm before Odysseus woke;
sentences.n: τὰ μὲν οὖν ‘so these things’ rounds off the unloading; αὐτοί in the next line begins the crew’s own movement. πυθμέν’ is πυθμένα, ‘base, trunk’, and ἐλαίης is ‘of the olive’; ἀθρόα, neuter plural, agrees with the goods, ‘all together, in a heap’; θῆκαν is the aorist of τίθημι. μή πώς … δηλήσαιτο ‘lest in some way … do harm’ is a negative purpose clause after a past verb, with the aorist optative of δηλέομαι ‘harm, damage’. ὁδιτάων is the epic genitive plural of ὁδίτης ‘wayfarer’, from ὁδός ‘road’. πρίν with the infinitive, πρὶν … ἔγρεσθαι, is ‘before … woke’, ἔγρεσθαι being the aorist middle infinitive of ἐγείρω. Ὀδυσῆ’ is Ὀδυσῆα with elision: the name has a spelling with σσ (Ὀδυσσῆα, line 117) and one with a single σ, to suit the verse.

sentences.t: αὐτοὶ δ’ αὖτ’ οἶκόνδε πάλιν κίον.
sentences.tr: autoi d’ aut’ oikonde palin kion.
sentences.l: And they themselves, in turn, homeward back went.
sentences.i: Then they themselves went back home.
sentences.n: αὐτοί ‘they themselves’ sets the men against the goods they have just left, and αὖτ’ is αὖτε ‘in turn, then’. οἶκόνδε is ‘homeward’, from οἶκον with the suffix -δε of direction, and πάλιν ‘back’. κίον is the past tense of κίω ‘go’, an epic verb of going. The unit ends at the full stop in the middle of line 125.

sentences.t:
οὐδ’ ἐνοσίχθων
λήθετ’ ἀπειλάων, τὰς ἀντιθέῳ Ὀδυσῆϊ
πρῶτον ἐπηπείλησε, Διὸς δ’ ἐξείρετο βουλήν·
sentences.tr:
oud’ enosichthōn
lēthet’ apeilaōn, tas antitheōi Odysēï
prōton epēpeilēse, Dios d’ exeireto boulēn·
sentences.l:
Nor did the earth-shaker
forget the threats, which to godlike Odysseus
he had first threatened, and Zeus’ plan he inquired into:
sentences.i: Nor did the earth-shaker forget the threats he had made earlier against godlike Odysseus, but inquired into the plan of Zeus:
sentences.n: ἐνοσίχθων ‘earth-shaker’ is Poseidon, named here by his title alone. λήθετ’ is λήθετο, an unaugmented imperfect of λήθομαι ‘forget’, which takes the genitive ἀπειλάων, the epic genitive plural of ἀπειλή ‘threat’. τάς … ἐπηπείλησε is a relative clause with a cognate object, ‘the threats which he threatened’, and πρῶτον ‘first’ looks back to the earlier threats, which are not repeated here. ἀντιθέῳ Ὀδυσῆϊ is the dative of the person threatened; ἀντίθεος is ‘godlike’. ἐξείρετο is the imperfect of ἐξείρομαι (εἴρομαι ‘ask’ with ἐκ-), ‘inquire into’, with Διὸς … βουλήν ‘the plan of Zeus’ as its object. The ano teleia leads into his speech.

sentences.t:
Ζεῦ πάτερ, οὐκέτ’ ἐγώ γε μετ’ ἀθανάτοισι θεοῖσι
τιμήεις ἔσομαι, ὅτε με βροτοὶ οὔ τι τίουσιν,
Φαίηκες, τοί πέρ τοι ἐμῆς ἔξ εἰσι γενέθλης.
sentences.tr:
Zeu pater, ouket’ egō ge met’ athanatoisi theoisi
timēeis esomai, hote me brotoi ou ti tiousin,
Phaiēkes, toi per toi emēs ex eisi genethlēs.
sentences.l:
“Father Zeus, no longer I among the immortal gods
honoured shall be, when me mortals in no way honour,
the Phaeacians, who indeed, you know, from my stock are.
sentences.i: “Father Zeus, I shall no longer be honoured among the immortal gods, when mortals do not honour me at all, the Phaeacians, who are, you know, of my stock.
sentences.n: Poseidon is the speaker, and his words are for Zeus: Ζεῦ πάτερ is ‘Father Zeus’. His complaint is about τιμή ‘honour’: τιμήεις ‘honoured’ and τίουσιν ‘they honour’ come from the same root, and the Phaeacians stand in apposition to βροτοί ‘mortals’. οὐκέτ’ … ἔσομαι is ‘I shall no longer be’, and οὔ τι ‘not at all’ is an adverbial accusative. ἀθανάτοισι θεοῖσι has the dative plural in -οισι. τοί … ἔξ εἰσι: τοί is here the relative ‘who’ (epic τοί for οἵ), and the second τοι is either σοι ‘to you’ or the particle ‘you know’, two readings the form cannot separate. ἔξ is ἐξ before εἰσι, and ἐμῆς … γενέθλης is ‘of my stock’, with γενέθλη ‘race, stock’.

sentences.t:
καὶ γὰρ νῦν Ὀδυσῆ’ ἐφάμην κακὰ πολλὰ παθόντα
οἴκαδ’ ἐλεύσεσθαι·
sentences.tr:
kai gar nyn Odysē’ ephamēn kaka polla pathonta
oikad’ eleusesthai·
sentences.l:
For indeed now I said that Odysseus, many evils having suffered,
would come homeward;
sentences.i: Why, even now: I said that Odysseus, once he had suffered many evils, would come home;
sentences.n: ἐφάμην is the imperfect middle of φημί, ‘I said’ (it can also mean ‘I supposed’), and it takes an accusative with the future infinitive ἐλεύσεσθαι: ‘that Odysseus would come’. Ὀδυσῆ’ is the elided Ὀδυσῆα, and κακὰ πολλὰ παθόντα, the aorist participle of πάσχω, agrees with it: ‘after suffering many evils’. οἴκαδ’ is ‘homeward’, with the suffix -δε. καὶ γὰρ νῦν is ‘for even now’, ‘in the present case’. The unit ends at the ano teleia in the middle of line 132.

sentences.t:
νόστον δέ οἱ οὔ ποτ’ ἀπηύρων
πάγχυ, ἐπεὶ σὺ πρῶτον ὑπέσχεο καὶ κατένευσας.
sentences.tr:
noston de hoi ou pot’ apēurōn
panchy, epei sy prōton hypescheo kai kateneusas.
sentences.l:
and his homecoming from him I never took away
altogether, since you first promised and nodded assent.
sentences.i: and I never took his homecoming from him altogether, since at first you promised it and nodded your assent.
sentences.n: ἀπηύρων is the imperfect of ἀπαυράω ‘take away’, with νόστον as its object and the dative οἱ ‘from him’; the negative οὔ ποτε ‘never’ is limited by πάγχυ ‘altogether’, so the claim is that he never took the homecoming away entirely. ὑπέσχεο is the aorist middle of ὑπισχνέομαι ‘promise’, with the uncontracted ending -εο for -ου. κατένευσας, the aorist of κατανεύω ‘nod down’, names the nod of assent that makes a promise binding. πρῶτον ‘first, at first’ points to the original promise. The unit begins mid-line.

sentences.t:
οἱ δ’ εὕδοντ’ ἐν νηῒ θοῇ ἐπὶ πόντον ἄγοντες
κάτθεσαν εἰν Ἰθάκῃ, ἔδοσαν δέ οἱ ἄσπετα δῶρα,
sentences.tr:
hoi d’ heudont’ en nēï thoēi epi ponton agontes
katthesan ein Ithakēi, edosan de hoi aspeta dōra,
sentences.l:
But they, him sleeping in a swift ship over the open-sea conveying,
set down in Ithaca, and gave him boundless gifts,
sentences.i: but while he slept they carried him over the sea in a swift ship and set him down in Ithaca, and gave him boundless gifts,
sentences.n: οἱ δ’ ‘but they’ is the Phaeacians again. εὕδοντ’ is εὕδοντα, the accusative singular participle ‘sleeping’, with ‘him’ understood as the object of ἄγοντες ‘conveying’ and κάτθεσαν; English has to say it. νηῒ θοῇ is ‘a swift ship’, and ἐπὶ πόντον with the accusative ‘over the open sea’. κάτθεσαν is κατέθεσαν with the vowel of the middle syllable lost, ‘set down’; εἰν is ἐν, and Ἰθάκῃ is the dative of Ἰθάκη. ἄσπετα is ‘boundless’, literally ‘not to be told’. The unit stops at a comma because the sentence runs to line 138.

sentences.t:
χαλκόν τε χρυσόν τε ἅλις ἐσθῆτά θ’ ὑφαντήν,
πόλλ’, ὅσ’ ἂν οὐδέ ποτε Τροίης ἐξήρατ’ Ὀδυσσεύς,
εἴ περ ἀπήμων ἦλθε, λαχὼν ἀπὸ ληΐδος αἶσαν.
sentences.tr:
chalkon te chryson te halis esthēta th’ hyphantēn,
poll’, hos’ an oude pote Troiēs exērat’ Odysseus,
ei per apēmōn ēlthe, lachōn apo lēïdos aisan.
sentences.l:
bronze and gold in abundance, and clothing woven,
much, such as never even from Troy would Odysseus have carried off,
even if unharmed he had come, having taken his share of the spoil.”
sentences.i: bronze and gold in plenty and woven clothing, more than Odysseus would ever have carried off from Troy itself, even if he had come home unharmed with his full share of the spoil.”
sentences.n: The three objects, χαλκόν … χρυσόν … ἐσθῆτα, stand in apposition to ἄσπετα δῶρα, and ἅλις is ‘in abundance’; ὑφαντήν is ‘woven’, and θ’ is τε. The second and third lines say how much: πόλλ’, ὅσ’ ἂν οὐδέ ποτε … ἐξήρατ’ is ‘much, such as he would never have carried off’, a past potential, ἄν with the aorist indicative of ἐξαίρω ‘lift out, take for oneself’. εἴ περ ἀπήμων ἦλθε is ‘even if he had come unharmed’, with ἀπήμων ‘unharmed’ from πῆμα ‘woe’. λαχών is the aorist participle of λαγχάνω ‘obtain as one’s lot’, ληΐδος the genitive of ληΐς ‘booty’, and αἶσα ‘share, due portion’. Τροίης has Ionic η. Poseidon’s speech ends here.

sentences.t: τὸν δ’ ἀπαμειβόμενος προσέφη νεφεληγερέτα Ζεύς·
sentences.tr: ton d’ apameibomenos prosephē nephelēgereta Zeus·
sentences.l: Him answering addressed cloud-gatherer Zeus:
sentences.i: In answer Zeus who gathers the clouds said to him:
sentences.n: A stock introduction to a reply: τὸν δ’ ‘and him’ (the article as a pronoun, accusative), ἀπαμειβόμενος ‘answering’ (a middle participle of ἀπαμείβομαι), and προσέφη ‘addressed’, the aorist of πρόσφημι. νεφεληγερέτα is a nominative in -α, an old form of nouns of agency in -της, ‘cloud-gatherer’. Zeus now takes the floor.

sentences.t: ὢ πόποι, ἐννοσίγαι’ εὐρυσθενές, οἷον ἔειπες.
sentences.tr: ō popoi, ennosigai’ eurysthenes, hoion eeipes.
sentences.l: “Ah, earth-shaker, of wide strength, what a thing you have said.
sentences.i: “Ah, earth-shaker, of far-reaching strength, what a thing you have said.
sentences.n: Zeus is speaking. ὢ πόποι is an exclamation of dismay or surprise, ‘Ah’. ἐννοσίγαι’ is the vocative of ἐννοσίγαιος ‘earth-shaker’, a compound built on γαῖα ‘earth’ (ἐνοσίχθων, used of Poseidon at 125 and 146, is built on χθών), and εὐρυσθενές the vocative of εὐρυσθενής ‘of wide strength’, from εὐρύς ‘wide’ and σθένος ‘strength’. οἷον ἔειπες is ‘what a thing you have said’: οἷον is the exclamatory neuter ‘of what sort’, and ἔειπες the epic form of εἶπες.

sentences.t: οὔ τί σ’ ἀτιμάζουσι θεοί·
sentences.tr: ou ti s’ atimazousi theoi·
sentences.l: Not at all do the gods dishonour you;
sentences.i: The gods do not dishonour you at all;
sentences.n: οὔ τι ‘not at all’ is an adverbial accusative, σ’ is σε, and ἀτιμάζουσι is built on τιμή ‘honour’ with the negative prefix ἀ-: Zeus answers Poseidon’s τιμήεις and τίουσιν (129) in kind. The unit ends at the ano teleia in the middle of line 141.

sentences.t:
χαλεπὸν δέ κεν εἴη
πρεσβύτατον καὶ ἄριστον ἀτιμίῃσιν ἰάλλειν.
sentences.tr:
chalepon de ken eiē
presbytaton kai ariston atimiēisin iallein.
sentences.l:
and hard it would be
the eldest and the best with dishonours to assail.
sentences.i: and it would be hard to assail the eldest and the best with dishonours.
sentences.n: κεν with the optative εἴη gives ‘it would be’. ἰάλλειν is ‘send, hurl’ and takes the dative ἀτιμίῃσιν ‘with dishonours’, the dative plural in -ῃσιν; so ‘to throw dishonours at’. πρεσβύτατον καὶ ἄριστον are accusatives, ‘the eldest and the best’, with σε ‘you’ understood as the object of the infinitive; πρεσβύτατος is the superlative of πρέσβυς ‘old’. The unit begins mid-line, after the ano teleia.

sentences.t:
ἀνδρῶν δ’ εἴ πέρ τίς σε βίῃ καὶ κάρτεϊ εἴκων
οὔ τι τίει.
sentences.tr:
andrōn d’ ei per tis se biēi kai karteï eikōn
ou ti tiei.
sentences.l:
But of men, if indeed anyone you, to force and might yielding,
does not at all honour,
sentences.i: But if any man, giving way to force and might, does not honour you at all,
sentences.n: εἰ πέρ τις is ‘if indeed anyone’, and ἀνδρῶν ‘of men’ is a partitive genitive. εἴκων is the present participle of εἴκω ‘give way to’, with the datives βίῃ καὶ κάρτεϊ ‘force and might’ (κάρτος is the epic form of κράτος); the Greek does not say whose force and might, and English leaves it open too. τίει is ‘honours’, from τίω, the same verb as τίουσιν in 129. The Greek has a full stop here, but the ‘if’ clause is completed by the next unit, so the English carries on with a comma.

sentences.t: σοὶ δ’ ἐστὶ καὶ ἐξοπίσω τίσις αἰεί.
sentences.tr: soi d’ esti kai exopisō tisis aiei.
sentences.l: to you there is, even afterwards, vengeance always.
sentences.i: you have vengeance always, even afterwards.
sentences.n: This is the main clause to which the ‘if’ clause of the last unit belongs; δέ marks the apodosis. τίσις is ‘vengeance, payment’, from τίνω ‘pay’, and ἐξοπίσω is ‘afterwards, in the future’ (ἐξ and ὀπίσω); καὶ ἐξοπίσω ‘even later’ is Zeus’s reassurance that a slight does not go unpaid. αἰεί is the epic form of ἀεί ‘always’. The unit begins in the middle of line 144.

sentences.t: ἔρξον ὅπως ἐθέλεις καί τοι φίλον ἔπλετο θυμῷ.
sentences.tr: erxon hopōs etheleis kai toi philon epleto thymōi.
sentences.l: Do as you wish, and as to you dear it has come to be in your heart.”
sentences.i: Do as you wish, and as is dear to your heart.”
sentences.n: ἔρξον is the aorist imperative of ἔρδω ‘do’, and ὅπως ἐθέλεις ‘as you wish’ gives its manner. τοι is σοι ‘to you’. ἔπλετο is an aorist of πέλομαι ‘come to be’ used where English has a present, ‘has come to be dear’, that is, ‘is dear’; θυμῷ is ‘in your heart’. With this permission Zeus’s first speech ends.

sentences.t: τὸν δ’ ἠμείβετ’ ἔπειτα Ποσειδάων ἐνοσίχθων·
sentences.tr: ton d’ ēmeibet’ epeita Poseidaōn enosichthōn·
sentences.l: Him then answered Poseidon earth-shaker:
sentences.i: Then Poseidon earth-shaker answered him:
sentences.n: The reply formula: τὸν δ’ ἠμείβετ’ ἔπειτα ‘and then he answered him’, with ἠμείβετο the imperfect of ἀμείβομαι ‘answer’. Ποσειδάων has the epic lengthened ending, and ἐνοσίχθων ‘earth-shaker’ is built on ἔνοσις ‘shaking’ and χθών ‘earth’.

sentences.t: αἶψά κ’ ἐγὼν ἔρξαιμι, κελαινεφές, ὡς ἀγορεύεις·
sentences.tr: aipsa k’ egōn erxaimi, kelainephes, hōs agoreueis·
sentences.l: “Quickly would I do it, dark-clouded one, as you say;
sentences.i: “I would do it quickly, you of the dark clouds, as you say;
sentences.n: κ’ is κε(ν), the same as ἄν, and with the aorist optative ἔρξαιμι it gives ‘I would do’. ἐγών is the epic form of ἐγώ. κελαινεφές is the vocative of κελαινεφής ‘dark-clouded’, a title of Zeus here used as direct address, from κελαινός ‘dark’ and νέφος ‘cloud’. ὡς ἀγορεύεις ‘as you say’ refers to the permission just given.

sentences.t: ἀλλὰ σὸν αἰεὶ θυμὸν ὀπίζομαι ἠδ’ ἀλεείνω.
sentences.tr: alla son aiei thymon opizomai ēd’ aleeinō.
sentences.l: but your heart I always stand in awe of and avoid.
sentences.i: but I always stand in awe of your heart, and keep clear of it.
sentences.n: ὀπίζομαι ‘I regard with awe’ and ἀλεείνω ‘I shun, I keep clear of’ share the one object, σὸν … θυμόν ‘your heart’, taken as the seat of anger and will; the traditional senses are followed, the first being the less certain. ἠδ’ is ἠδέ ‘and’, and αἰεί ‘always’. The unit gives Poseidon’s reason for asking leave before he acts.

sentences.t:
νῦν αὖ Φαιήκων ἐθέλω περικαλλέα νῆα,
ἐκ πομπῆς ἀνιοῦσαν, ἐν ἠεροειδέϊ πόντῳ
ῥαῖσαι, ἵν’ ἤδη σχῶνται, ἀπολλήξωσι δὲ πομπῆς
ἀνθρώπων, μέγα δέ σφιν ὄρος πόλει ἀμφικαλύψαι.
sentences.tr:
nyn au Phaiēkōn ethelō perikallea nēa,
ek pompēs aniousan, en ēeroeideï pontōi
rhaisai, hin’ ēdē schōntai, apollēxōsi de pompēs
anthrōpōn, mega de sphin oros polei amphikalypsai.
sentences.l:
Now in turn of the Phaeacians I wish a very fair ship,
coming back from an escort, on the misty-looking sea,
to smash, so that now they may check themselves and cease from escorting
men, and a great mountain for them over their city to enfold.”
sentences.i: Now, in my turn, I want to smash a very fair ship of the Phaeacians as she comes back from an escort on the misty-looking sea, so that they may now hold themselves back and cease from escorting men, and to enfold their city in a great mountain.”
sentences.n: The wish is expressed by ἐθέλω ‘I wish’ with two infinitives, ῥαῖσαι ‘to smash’ (from ῥαίω) and ἀμφικαλύψαι ‘to enfold’ (the second joined by δέ); the purpose clause between them has the aorist subjunctives σχῶνται ‘may check themselves’ (from ἔχω) and ἀπολλήξωσι ‘may leave off’, which takes the genitive πομπῆς ἀνθρώπων ‘escorting of men’. νῦν αὖ is ‘now in turn’, and Φαιήκων goes with νῆα, whose epithet is περικαλλέα ‘very fair’. ἐκ πομπῆς ἀνιοῦσαν is ‘coming back from an escort’, the ship returning after taking a guest home. ἠεροειδέϊ ‘misty-looking’ is built on ἀήρ ‘mist’, and its dative has the two final vowels apart. μέγα … ὄρος is the object of ἀμφικαλύψαι, with σφιν ‘for them’ and πόλει ‘over their city’ as datives.

sentences.t: τὸν δ’ ἀπαμειβόμενος προσέφη νεφεληγερέτα Ζεύς·
sentences.tr: ton d’ apameibomenos prosephē nephelēgereta Zeus·
sentences.l: Him answering addressed cloud-gatherer Zeus:
sentences.i: In answer Zeus who gathers the clouds said to him:
sentences.n: The same reply formula as at line 139, with the same English. Zeus now answers Poseidon’s plan.

sentences.t: ὢ πέπον, ὡς μὲν ἐμῷ θυμῷ δοκεῖ εἶναι ἄριστα,
sentences.tr: ō pepon, hōs men emōi thymōi dokei einai arista,
sentences.l: “O good one, as to my heart it seems to be best,
sentences.i: “My good fellow, as it seems best to my heart,
sentences.n: ὢ πέπον is a form of address; the meaning of πέπον is not known (‘ripe’, ‘soft’ and ‘dear’ have all been proposed), and ‘good’ is only a placeholder. ὡς μὲν ἐμῷ θυμῷ δοκεῖ εἶναι ἄριστα is ‘as it seems to my heart to be best’, the dative ἐμῷ θυμῷ giving the one to whom it seems, and ἄριστα the neuter plural ‘best things’. The unit stops at a comma because the sentence runs to line 158, five lines.

sentences.t:
ὁππότε κεν δὴ πάντες ἐλαυνομένην προΐδωνται
λαοὶ ἀπὸ πτόλιος, θεῖναι λίθον ἐγγύθι γαίης
νηῒ θοῇ ἴκελον, ἵνα θαυμάζωσιν ἅπαντες
ἄνθρωποι, μέγα δέ σφιν ὄρος πόλει ἀμφικαλύψαι.
sentences.tr:
hoppote ken dē pantes elaunomenēn proïdōntai
laoi apo ptolios, theinai lithon engythi gaiēs
nēï thoēi ikelon, hina thaumazōsin hapantes
anthrōpoi, mega de sphin oros polei amphikalypsai.
sentences.l:
whenever indeed all, her being driven on, catch sight of from afar,
the people from the city, to make a stone near the land
like a swift ship, so that they marvel, all
men, and a great mountain for them over their city to enfold.”
sentences.i: when all the people have caught sight of her from the city as she is driven on, to make a stone near the land in the likeness of a swift ship, so that all men may marvel, and to enfold their city in a great mountain.”
sentences.n: The two infinitives θεῖναι ‘to make’ (aorist of τίθημι) and ἀμφικαλύψαι ‘to enfold’ both rest on δοκεῖ … ἄριστα: ‘it seems best … to do this and that’. ὁππότε κεν … προΐδωνται is ‘whenever they catch sight of’, the aorist subjunctive middle of προοράω ‘see from afar’; ἐλαυνομένην is the passive participle ‘as she is driven’. πτόλιος is the epic genitive of πτόλις, a by-form of πόλις. ἴκελον ‘like’ takes the dative νηῒ θοῇ, and ἐγγύθι ‘near’ is ἐγγύς with the place-suffix -θι. The last line, from μέγα δέ on, is word for word Poseidon’s line 152 (which opens with ἀνθρώπων where this has ἄνθρωποι) and has the same English; Zeus keeps the mountain but turns the smashing into a stone ship.

sentences.t:
αὐτὰρ ἐπεὶ τό γ’ ἄκουσε Ποσειδάων ἐνοσίχθων,
βῆ ῥ’ ἴμεν ἐς Σχερίην, ὅθι Φαίηκες γεγάασιν.
sentences.tr:
autar epei to g’ akouse Poseidaōn enosichthōn,
bē rh’ imen es Scheriēn, hothi Phaiēkes gegaasin.
sentences.l:
But when that he heard, Poseidon earth-shaker,
he set out to go to Scheria, where the Phaeacians have come to be.
sentences.i: But when Poseidon earth-shaker heard that, he set out for Scheria, where the Phaeacians have their home.
sentences.n: τό γ’ ‘that’ is the plan Zeus has just stated. βῆ ῥ’ ἴμεν is the formula ‘set out to go’: βῆ is the aorist of βαίνω, ἴμεν the epic infinitive of εἶμι, and ῥ’ is ῥα. Σχερίην is Scheria, the Phaeacians’ land, in the accusative of goal after ἐς. γεγάασιν is the perfect of γίγνομαι ‘have come to be’, here ‘are there, have their home’; ὅθι is ‘where’.

sentences.t: ἔνθ’ ἔμεν’·
sentences.tr: enth’ emen’·
sentences.l: There he waited;
sentences.i: There he waited;
sentences.n: ἔμεν’ is ἔμενε, the imperfect of μένω ‘wait, stay’: Poseidon waits in Scheria while the ship approaches, and the stop after so short a clause sets the waiting against what follows. ἔνθα ‘there’ is Scheria. The unit is the shortest kind, ending at an ano teleia in the middle of line 161.

sentences.t:
ἡ δὲ μάλα σχεδὸν ἤλυθε ποντοπόρος νηῦς
ῥίμφα διωκομένη·
sentences.tr:
hē de mala schedon ēlythe pontoporos nēus
rhimpha diōkomenē·
sentences.l:
and she very close came, the sea-crossing ship,
nimbly being driven on;
sentences.i: while she, the sea-crossing ship, came very close, driven nimbly on;
sentences.n: ἡ δέ ‘and she’ is the ship, set against Poseidon waiting. ἤλυθε is the epic form of ἦλθε, σχεδόν ‘near’, and ποντοπόρος ‘sea-crossing’ is built on πόντος ‘open sea’ and πόρος ‘passage’. διωκομένη is the passive participle of διώκω ‘pursue, drive on’, and ῥίμφα ‘nimbly’ is an adverb of light, quick motion.

sentences.t:
τῆς δὲ σχεδὸν ἦλθ’ ἐνοσίχθων,
ὅς μιν λᾶαν ἔθηκε καὶ ἐρρίζωσεν ἔνερθε
χειρὶ καταπρηνεῖ ἐλάσας·
sentences.tr:
tēs de schedon ēlth’ enosichthōn,
hos min laan ethēke kai errizōsen enerthe
cheiri kataprēnei elasas·
sentences.i: and the earth-shaker came close to her, and he turned her into a stone and rooted her fast beneath, striking with the flat of his hand;
sentences.n: The subject is Poseidon, who has now come up to the ship, and the relative clause ὅς … says what he did. ἔθηκε is the aorist of τίθημι with a double accusative, μιν … λᾶαν ‘made her a stone’, λᾶας being ‘stone’. ἐρρίζωσεν is ‘rooted’, from ῥιζόω; the doubled ρ is the augment fused with the initial ῥ. ἔνερθε is ‘beneath’. χειρὶ καταπρηνεῖ is ‘with a hand turned down’, καταπρηνής meaning ‘turned downward’, so that the blow comes from above, and ἐλάσας, the aorist participle of ἐλαύνω, is here ‘striking’. The unit ends at the ano teleia in the middle of line 164.

sentences.t: ὁ δὲ νόσφι βεβήκει.
sentences.tr: ho de nosphi bebēkei.
sentences.l: and he apart had gone away.
sentences.i: and he had gone off.
sentences.n: ὁ δέ ‘and he’ is Poseidon, set against the ship. βεβήκει is the pluperfect of βαίνω, ‘had gone’ (Attic ἐβεβήκει), and νόσφι ‘apart, away’. The pluperfect has Poseidon already gone when the Phaeacians react.

sentences.t:
οἱ δὲ πρὸς ἀλλήλους ἔπεα πτερόεντ’ ἀγόρευον
Φαίηκες δολιχήρετμοι, ναυσίκλυτοι ἄνδρες.
sentences.tr:
hoi de pros allēlous epea pteroent’ agoreuon
Phaiēkes dolichēretmoi, nausiklytoi andres.
sentences.l:
And they to one another winged words spoke,
the long-oared Phaeacians, ship-famous men.
sentences.i: And the long-oared Phaeacians, men famous for their ships, spoke winged words to one another.
sentences.n: οἱ δέ ‘and they’ are the Phaeacians, named in the next line. ἔπεα πτερόεντα ‘winged words’ is the stock phrase for words that fly from speaker to hearer, here with ἀγόρευον ‘spoke’ and πρὸς ἀλλήλους ‘to one another’. δολιχήρετμοι is ‘long-oared’, from δολιχός ‘long’ and ἐρετμόν ‘oar’, and ναυσίκλυτοι ‘famous for their ships’, from ναῦς and κλυτός ‘famous’; the whole line 166 is a formula for the Phaeacians.

sentences.t: ὧδε δέ τις εἴπεσκεν ἰδὼν ἐς πλησίον ἄλλον·
sentences.tr: hōde de tis eipesken idōn es plēsion allon·
sentences.l: And thus someone would say, looking to another close by:
sentences.i: And as each looked at the one beside him, he would say something like this:
sentences.n: ὧδε ‘thus’ introduces the words of the speech. εἴπεσκεν is the iterative of εἶπον, formed with -σκ-, ‘would say’: each man says it in turn to his neighbour, so the speech that follows stands for many voices. ἰδών is ‘looking’ and πλησίον, an adverb, is used as an adjective, ‘one close by’.

sentences.t:
ὤ μοι, τίς δὴ νῆα θοὴν ἐπέδησ’ ἐνὶ πόντῳ
οἴκαδ’ ἐλαυνομένην;
sentences.tr:
ō moi, tis dē nēa thoēn epedēs’ eni pontōi
oikad’ elaunomenēn;
sentences.l:
“Oh me, who now the swift ship has bound on the open-sea
as she was driven homeward?
sentences.i: “Oh me! Who has bound the swift ship on the sea as she was driven homeward?
sentences.n: The speaker is anonymous, one of the Phaeacians, a τις ‘someone’ as the line before promised. ὤ μοι is ‘oh me’, a cry of dismay. ἐπέδησ’ is ἐπέδησε, the aorist of ἐπιδέω ‘bind on’ (or of πεδάω ‘fetter’, from πέδη ‘fetter’, which is spelled the same): the ship is held fast as if shackled. νῆα is the Ionic accusative of νηῦς, and ἐλαυνομένην, a passive participle agreeing with it, is ‘as she was being driven’; οἴκαδ’ is ‘homeward’. The unit ends at the question mark in the middle of line 169.

sentences.t: καὶ δὴ προὐφαίνετο πᾶσα.
sentences.tr: kai dē prouphaineto pasa.
sentences.l: And indeed she was appearing forth, all of her.”
sentences.i: And already she was showing herself in full view.”
sentences.n: προὐφαίνετο is the imperfect middle of προφαίνομαι ‘show forth, come into view’, with the preverb and the augment fused (προ- + ἐφαίνετο). καὶ δή is ‘and indeed, and already’, and πᾶσα ‘all of her’ agrees with the ship. The point of the whole question is that she was in plain sight, close to the land, when she was stopped. The unit begins after the question mark, mid-line.

sentences.t: ὣς ἄρα τις εἴπεσκε·
sentences.tr: hōs ara tis eipeske·
sentences.l: So then someone would say;
sentences.i: So one of them would say;
sentences.n: εἴπεσκε is the same iterative ‘would say’ as εἴπεσκεν in line 167, which closes the frame: the speech has been given by many, one after another. ὣς ἄρα is ‘so then’, the formula that rounds off a speech. The unit ends at the ano teleia in the middle of line 170.

sentences.t: τὰ δ’ οὐκ ἴσαν ὡς ἐτέτυκτο.
sentences.tr: ta d’ ouk isan hōs etetykto.
sentences.l: but they did not know how it had been contrived.
sentences.i: not knowing how matters really stood.
sentences.n: τὰ δ’ οὐκ ἴσαν is ‘but they did not know (it)’: ἴσαν is the old pluperfect of οἶδα, ‘they knew’, and τά ‘these things’ is its object. ὡς ἐτέτυκτο is ‘how it had been made’, the pluperfect passive of τεύχω ‘make, bring about’: the Phaeacians do not know that a god has done this. The unit begins in the middle of line 170.

sentences.t: τοῖσιν δ’ Ἀλκίνοος ἀγορήσατο καὶ μετέειπεν·
sentences.tr: toisin d’ Alkinoos agorēsato kai meteeipen·
sentences.l: To them Alcinous addressed-the-assembly and spoke among them:
sentences.i: Alcinous addressed the assembly and spoke among them:
sentences.n: τοῖσιν ‘to them’ is the dative plural of the pronoun, with -οισιν. ἀγορήσατο ‘addressed the assembly’ comes from ἀγορή ‘assembly’, and μετέειπεν ‘spoke among them’ from μετά ‘among’ and εἶπον, with movable ν; together they are the stock opening for a man who rises to speak to a gathering. Alcinous is named here without a title.

sentences.t:
ὢ πόποι, ἦ μάλα δή με παλαίφατα θέσφαθ’ ἱκάνει
πατρὸς ἐμοῦ, ὃς ἔφασκε Ποσειδάων’ ἀγάσασθαι
ἡμῖν, οὕνεκα πομποὶ ἀπήμονές εἰμεν ἁπάντων.
sentences.tr:
ō popoi, ē mala dē me palaiphata thesphath’ hikanei
patros emou, hos ephaske Poseidaōn’ agasasthai
hēmin, houneka pompoi apēmones eimen hapantōn.
sentences.l:
“Ah, truly indeed now me the long-ago-spoken god-declared things are reaching,
of my father, who used-to-say that Poseidon was resentful
of us, because escorts harmless we are of all.
sentences.i: “Ah, the prophecies of my father, spoken long ago, are truly coming upon me now; he used to say that Poseidon resented us because we are harmless escorts of all men.
sentences.n: Alcinous is speaking. παλαίφατα θέσφαθ’ is ‘prophecies spoken long ago’: παλαίφατος is ‘spoken of old’ (πάλαι ‘long ago’ and φατός), and θέσφατα are ‘things declared by a god’, with the τ of θέσφατ’ turned to θ before the rough breathing of ἱκάνει. The neuter plural subject takes a singular verb, ἱκάνει ‘reaches’, as it would in Attic. πατρὸς ἐμοῦ ‘of my father’ belongs with the prophecies. ἔφασκε is the iterative ‘used to say’, and ἀγάσασθαι ‘to be resentful of’ takes the dative ἡμῖν. Ποσειδάων’ is the accusative Ποσειδάωνα with elision. ἀπήμονες ‘harmless’ is built on πῆμα ‘woe’; εἰμεν is the epic form of ἐσμέν, and ἁπάντων ‘of all’ means all men.

sentences.t:
φῆ ποτὲ Φαιήκων ἀνδρῶν περικαλλέα, νῆα,
ἐκ πομπῆς ἀνιοῦσαν, ἐν ἠεροειδέϊ πόντῳ
ῥαισέμεναι, μέγα δ’ ἧμιν ὄρος πόλει ἀμφικαλύψειν.
sentences.tr:
phē pote Phaiēkōn andrōn perikallea, nēa,
ek pompēs aniousan, en ēeroeideï pontōi
rhaisemenai, mega d’ hēmin oros polei amphikalypsein.
sentences.l:
He said that some day of the Phaeacian men a very fair ship,
coming back from an escort, on the misty-looking sea
he would smash, and a great mountain over our city would enfold.
sentences.i: He said that some day he would smash a very fair ship of the Phaeacian men as she came back from an escort on the misty-looking sea, and would enfold our city in a great mountain.
sentences.n: φῆ is ἔφη ‘he said’, and the old man’s words are reported with the future infinitives ῥαισέμεναι ‘would smash’ (the ending -μεναι is epic; Attic would have ῥαίσειν) and ἀμφικαλύψειν ‘would enfold’; the subject, Poseidon, is carried over from line 173. ποτέ is ‘some day’. The prophecy is Poseidon’s own plan of lines 149–152 almost word for word, which is what Alcinous recognises, and the ship is again περικαλλέα ‘very fair’. ἧμιν is ἡμῖν. The printed text has a comma after περικαλλέα, separating the adjective from its noun without changing the sense.

sentences.t: ὣς ἀγόρευ’ ὁ γέρων· τὰ δὲ δὴ νῦν πάντα τελεῖται.
sentences.tr: hōs agoreu’ ho gerōn· ta de dē nyn panta teleitai.
sentences.l: So the old man spoke, and now indeed all these things are being fulfilled.
sentences.i: So the old man spoke, and now all of it is being fulfilled.
sentences.n: ὁ γέρων ‘the old man’ is Alcinous’ father, whose words have just been quoted, and ἀγόρευ’ is ἀγόρευε, the imperfect of ἀγορεύω ‘speak’. τά is ‘these things’, a neuter plural, and δὴ νῦν ‘now indeed’. τελεῖται is the present passive of τελέω ‘bring to an end, fulfil’, with a present sense, ‘is being brought to pass’. The same verb returns at 212 in the negative, οὐδ’ ἐτέλεσσαν, where Odysseus says the Phaeacians did not fulfil their word. The old man’s words are over, but Alcinous’ own speech runs on to 183.

sentences.t: ἀλλ’ ἄγεθ’, ὡς ἂν ἐγὼ εἴπω, πειθώμεθα πάντες·
sentences.tr: all’ ageth’, hōs an egō eipō, peithōmetha pantes·
sentences.l: But come, as I may say, let us obey, all of us;
sentences.i: But come, let us all do as I say;
sentences.n: ἄγεθ’ is the plural imperative ἄγετε ‘come’, used as an exhortation. ὡς ἂν ἐγὼ εἴπω is ‘as I shall say’, with ὡς, ἄν and the aorist subjunctive. πειθώμεθα is the present subjunctive middle, a call to action, ‘let us obey’, the one obeyed being left unstated. The ano teleia leads into the instructions.

sentences.t:
πομπῆς μὲν παύσασθε βροτῶν, ὅτε κέν τις ἵκηται
ἡμέτερον προτὶ ἄστυ·
sentences.tr:
pompēs men pausasthe brotōn, hote ken tis hikētai
hēmeteron proti asty·
sentences.l:
From the escort of mortals cease, whenever anyone may come
to our town;
sentences.i: Stop escorting mortals whenever anyone comes to our town;
sentences.n: πομπῆς … παύσασθε is ‘cease from escorting’: παύσασθε is the aorist middle imperative of παύω, ‘cease’, which takes the genitive, and βροτῶν ‘of mortals’ depends on πομπῆς. ὅτε κέν τις ἵκηται is ‘whenever anyone comes’, a general clause with ὅτε, κε and the aorist subjunctive. προτί is πρός ‘to’, and ἄστυ ‘town’. μέν is answered by δέ in the next unit.

sentences.t:
Ποσειδάωνι δὲ ταύρους
δώδεκα κεκριμένους ἱερεύσομεν, αἴ κ’ ἐλεήσῃ,
μηδ’ ἡμῖν περίμηκες ὄρος πόλει ἀμφικαλύψῃ.
sentences.tr:
Poseidaōni de taurous
dōdeka kekrimenous hiereusomen, ai k’ eleēsēi,
mēd’ hēmin perimēkes oros polei amphikalypsēi.
sentences.l:
And to Poseidon bulls
twelve, picked out, we will sacrifice, if he may take pity,
and not for us a very long mountain over our city enfold.”
sentences.i: And we will sacrifice twelve picked bulls to Poseidon, in the hope that he will take pity and not enfold our city in a very long mountain.”
sentences.n: ἱερεύσομεν is ‘we will sacrifice’ (it could also be read as a short-vowel subjunctive, ‘let us sacrifice’), from ἱερεύω, and κεκριμένους, the perfect passive participle of κρίνω, is ‘picked out, chosen’. αἴ κ’ ἐλεήσῃ is ‘if he should take pity’, αἰ being εἰ and κε going with the aorist subjunctive; μηδ’ … ἀμφικαλύψῃ, a negative aorist subjunctive, continues the hope: ‘and not enfold’. περίμηκες is ‘very long’, with περι- intensive and μῆκος ‘length’, and σφιν has become ἡμῖν, ‘for us’, with πόλει ‘over our city’. Alcinous’ speech ends here.

sentences.t: ὣς ἔφαθ’, οἱ δ’ ἔδεισαν, ἑτοιμάσσαντο δὲ ταύρους.
sentences.tr: hōs ephath’, hoi d’ edeisan, hetoimassanto de taurous.
sentences.l: So he spoke, and they feared, and prepared the bulls.
sentences.i: So he spoke, and they were afraid, and made the bulls ready.
sentences.n: ὣς ἔφαθ’ is the closing formula ‘so he spoke’; ἔφαθ’ is ἔφατο, with the τ turned to θ before the rough breathing of οἱ. ἔδεισαν is the aorist of δείδω ‘fear’, and ἑτοιμάσσαντο the aorist middle of ἑτοιμάζω ‘make ready’, with the epic doubled σσ. The speech is over and the narrator resumes.

sentences.t:
ὣς οἱ μέν ῥ’ εὔχοντο Ποσειδάωνι ἄνακτι
δήμου Φαιήκων ἡγήτορες ἠδὲ μέδοντες,
ἑσταότες περὶ βωμόν.
sentences.tr:
hōs hoi men rh’ euchonto Poseidaōni anakti
dēmou Phaiēkōn hēgētores ēde medontes,
hestaotes peri bōmon.
sentences.l:
So they then prayed to Poseidon the lord,
the leaders and lords of the land of the Phaeacians,
standing around the altar.
sentences.i: So the leaders and lords of the Phaeacian land prayed to lord Poseidon, standing around the altar.
sentences.n: οἱ μέν ‘they, for their part’ is set against ὁ δέ ‘but he’ in the next unit, which turns to Odysseus. ῥ’ is ῥα, and εὔχοντο is the imperfect of εὔχομαι ‘pray’. Ποσειδάωνι ἄνακτι is ‘to Poseidon the lord’, ἄναξ meaning ‘lord’. δήμου Φαιήκων is ‘of the land of the Phaeacians’, δῆμος being rendered ‘land’; ἡγήτορες ‘leaders’ and μέδοντες ‘lords’ (from μέδω ‘rule’) are the same pair that Odysseus names in 210. ἑσταότες is the epic perfect participle of ἵστημι ‘standing’, and βωμός is ‘altar’, since a sacrifice is in view. The unit ends at the full stop in the middle of line 187.

sentences.t:
ὁ δ’ ἔγρετο δῖος Ὀδυσσεὺς
εὕδων ἐν γαίῃ πατρωΐῃ, οὐδέ μιν ἔγνω,
ἤδη δὴν ἀπεών·
sentences.tr:
ho d’ egreto dios Odysseus
heudōn en gaiēi patrōïēi, oude min egnō,
ēdē dēn apeōn·
sentences.i: But heavenly Odysseus woke from his sleep in his father’s land, and did not know it, after being away so long;
sentences.n: ὁ δ’ ‘but he’ turns from the Phaeacians at prayer to Odysseus; ἔγρετο is the aorist middle of ἐγείρω ‘wake up’, and εὕδων ‘sleeping’ names the state he wakes from. πατρωΐῃ is the feminine of πατρώϊος ‘of one’s father, ancestral’, the diaeresis showing that ω and ι are separate syllables. οὐδέ μιν ἔγνω is ‘and did not recognise it’: μιν is a pronoun that does not show gender, here the land. ἀπεών is the epic participle of ἄπειμι ‘be away’ (Attic ἀπών), and ἤδη δὴν ‘already long’. The unit ends at the ano teleia in the middle of line 189; the next gives the reason.

sentences.t:
περὶ γὰρ θεὸς ἠέρα χεῦε
Παλλὰς Ἀθηναίη, κούρη Διός, ὄφρα μιν αὐτὸν
ἄγνωστον τεύξειεν ἕκαστά τε μυθήσαιτο,
sentences.tr:
peri gar theos ēera cheue
Pallas Athēnaiē, kourē Dios, ophra min auton
agnōston teuxeien hekasta te mythēsaito,
sentences.i: For the goddess Pallas Athena, daughter of Zeus, had poured a mist around him, so that she might make him unrecognisable and tell him every detail,
sentences.n: περὶ … χεῦε is tmesis for περίχευε, ‘poured around (him)’; χεῦε is the unaugmented aorist of χέω ‘pour’, and ἠέρα is ‘mist’ (Ionic ἠήρ), not ‘air’. θεός is feminine here, ‘goddess’, in apposition with Παλλὰς Ἀθηναίη (Ionic Ἀθηναίη, Attic Ἀθηναία). The purpose clause with ὄφρα has two aorist optatives, τεύξειεν ‘might make’ (from τεύχω) and μυθήσαιτο ‘might tell’ (from μυθέομαι), and Athena is taken as the subject of both. ἄγνωστον ‘unknown’ is predicative, so that the sense is ‘make him unrecognisable’; μιν αὐτόν is ‘him himself’. ἕκαστα is ‘each thing’; the Greek gives no pronoun for the one told, and English adds ‘him’. The unit stops at a comma because the sentence runs to line 193.

sentences.t:
μή μιν πρὶν ἄλοχος γνοίη ἀστοί τε φίλοι τε,
πρὶν πᾶσαν μνηστῆρας ὑπερβασίην ἀποτῖσαι.
sentences.tr:
mē min prin alochos gnoiē astoi te philoi te,
prin pasan mnēstēras hyperbasiēn apotisai.
sentences.l:
lest him earlier his wife recognise, and townsmen and friends,
before the suitors all their overstepping pay back.
sentences.i: so that neither his wife nor his townsmen nor his friends would recognise him before the suitors had paid in full for all their transgression.
sentences.n: μή + optative γνοίη ‘lest … recognise’ continues the purpose clause, with μιν ‘him’. Its subjects are ἄλοχος ‘wife’ and ἀστοί τε φίλοι τε ‘townsmen and friends’, the last two joined by τε … τε; the wife is not named here. The first πρίν is an adverb, ‘before (that time)’, and the second takes the infinitive ἀποτῖσαι ‘pay back’, the aorist of ἀποτίνω, with μνηστῆρας ‘the suitors’ as its subject in the accusative. ὑπερβασίη ‘overstepping’ comes from ὑπερβαίνω ‘step over’, a crossing of the proper limit; πᾶσαν goes with it, ‘all their transgression’.

sentences.t:
τοὔνεκ’ ἄρ’ ἀλλοειδέα φαινέσκετο πάντα ἄνακτι,
ἀτραπιτοί τε διηνεκέες λιμένες τε πάνορμοι
πέτραι τ’ ἠλίβατοι καὶ δένδρεα τηλεθόωντα.
sentences.tr:
tounek’ ar’ alloeidea phainesketo panta anakti,
atrapitoi te diēnekees limenes te panormoi
petrai t’ ēlibatoi kai dendrea tēlethoōnta.
sentences.l:
For that reason other-looking appeared all things to the lord,
the paths unbroken, and the harbours all-mooring,
and the rocks towering, and the trees thriving.
sentences.i: That is why everything kept looking different to the lord: the unbroken paths, the harbours that give mooring everywhere, the towering rocks, and the thriving trees.
sentences.n: τοὔνεκ’ is τοῦ ἕνεκα ‘for that reason’ and points back to Athena’s mist. φαινέσκετο is the iterative imperfect of φαίνομαι ‘kept appearing’, and ἀλλοειδέα ‘other-looking’ is built on ἄλλος and εἶδος ‘form’; ἄνακτι ‘to the lord’ is Odysseus. The three lines are one thought, with the four things in apposition to πάντα. ἀτραπιτοί are ‘paths’, and διηνεκέες ‘unbroken, continuous’. λιμένες are ‘harbours’, and πάνορμοι is ‘all-mooring’, traditionally ‘good for mooring everywhere’; the sense is only approximately known. ἠλίβατοι ‘towering’ is a word whose meaning is not known; ‘steep, towering’ is the traditional guess. τηλεθόωντα is ‘thriving’, the participle with its two vowels uncontracted.

sentences.t: στῆ δ’ ἄρ’ ἀναΐξας καί ῥ’ εἴσιδε πατρίδα γαῖαν·
sentences.tr: stē d’ ar’ anaïxas kai rh’ eiside patrida gaian·
sentences.l: And he stood, having sprung up, and looked upon the fatherland;
sentences.i: He sprang up and stood, and looked upon the fatherland;
sentences.n: στῆ is the aorist of ἵστημι, ‘he stood’, and ἀναΐξας the aorist participle of ἀναΐσσω ‘spring up’, the diaeresis marking separate syllables. εἴσιδε is ‘looked upon, saw’ and ῥ’ is ῥα. πατρίδα γαῖαν is ‘fatherland’, with no possessive in the Greek. He sees the land but, as line 188 said, does not recognise it.

sentences.t:
ᾤμωξέν τ’ ἄρ ἔπειτα καὶ ὣ πεπλήγετο μηρὼ
χερσὶ καταπρηνέσσ’, ὀλοφυρόμενος δ’ ἔπος ηὔδα·
sentences.tr:
ōimōxen t’ ar epeita kai hō peplēgeto mērō
chersi kataprēness’, olophyromenos d’ epos ēuda·
sentences.l:
and cried out then, and struck his own two thighs
with downturned hands, and lamenting a word he spoke:
sentences.i: He cried out, and struck both his thighs with the flats of his hands, and as he lamented he spoke:
sentences.n: ᾤμωξεν is the aorist of οἰμώζω ‘cry out in grief’. ὣ … μηρώ is ‘his own two thighs’: ὣ is taken as the dual of the possessive ὅς ‘his own’, agreeing with the dual μηρώ, from μηρός ‘thigh’. πεπλήγετο is an epic reduplicated form of the middle of πλήσσω ‘strike’, and the middle marks that he struck himself, a gesture of grief. χερσὶ καταπρηνέσσ’ is ‘with hands turned down’, an elided dative plural in -εσσι. ὀλοφυρόμενος is ‘lamenting’, and ἔπος ηὔδα, literally ‘uttered a word’, introduces the speech.

sentences.t: ὤ μοι ἐγώ, τέων αὖτε βροτῶν ἐς γαῖαν ἱκάνω;
sentences.tr: ō moi egō, teōn aute brotōn es gaian hikanō;
sentences.l: “Oh me, I — of what mortals, this time, to the land do I come?
sentences.i: “Oh me! To the land of what mortals have I come this time?
sentences.n: Odysseus is speaking. ὤ μοι ἐγώ is ‘oh me, I’, with an emphatic ἐγώ. τέων is the epic genitive of τίς (Attic τίνων), ‘of what’, with βροτῶν ‘mortals’. αὖτε is ‘again, this time’, and ἱκάνω is the present ‘I come, arrive’. The question is about who lives in the land he has just woken in.

sentences.t:
ἦ ῥ’ οἵ γ’ ὑβρισταί τε καὶ ἄγριοι οὐδὲ δίκαιοι,
ἦε φιλόξεινοι, καί σφιν νόος ἐστὶ θεουδής;
sentences.tr:
ē rh’ hoi g’ hybristai te kai agrioi oude dikaioi,
ēe philoxeinoi, kai sphin noos esti theoudēs;
sentences.l:
Is it that they are violent and savage and not just,
or hospitable, and to them the mind is god-fearing?
sentences.i: Are they violent and savage and unjust, or kind to strangers, with a god-fearing mind?
sentences.n: ἦ ῥ’ is the question particle ‘is it that’, and οἵ γ’ is ‘they’, the pronoun, not the relative. ὑβρισταί ‘violent’ names men who commit ὕβρις; ἄγριοι is ‘savage’, and οὐδὲ δίκαιοι ‘nor just’. ἦε is ἠέ ‘or’, φιλόξεινοι ‘hospitable’ is built on φίλος and ξένος, and σφιν is ‘to them’. θεουδής ‘god-fearing’ is taken as θεός and δέος ‘fear’. The two lines set three bad qualities against two good. The printed text has a comma after φιλόξεινοι that does not change the sense.

sentences.t: πῇ δὴ χρήματα πολλὰ φέρω τάδε;
sentences.tr: pēi dē chrēmata polla pherō tade;
sentences.l: Where, now, these many goods am I to carry?
sentences.i: Where am I to carry all these goods?
sentences.n: πῇ δή is ‘where, then’. φέρω is a present form that is also the subjunctive, and the question is deliberative: ‘where am I to carry’. χρήματα are ‘goods, possessions’, neuter plural, here the Phaeacians’ gifts, which lie in a heap by the olive (122); τάδε ‘these here’ points at them. The unit ends at the question mark in the middle of line 203.

sentences.t:
πῇ τε καὶ αὐτὸς
πλάζομαι;
sentences.tr:
pēi te kai autos
plazomai;
sentences.l:
And where, too, I myself
am I driven astray?
sentences.i: And where am I myself being driven astray?
sentences.n: πλάζομαι ‘I am driven astray, I wander’ is the passive of πλάζω. πῇ τε καὶ αὐτός is ‘and where I myself’: τε καί joins this question to the one before, and αὐτός sets the man himself beside his goods. The unit begins in the middle of line 203, after the question mark.

sentences.t:
αἴθ’ ὄφελον μεῖναι παρὰ Φαιήκεσσιν
αὐτοῦ·
sentences.tr:
aith’ ophelon meinai para Phaiēkessin
autou·
sentences.l:
Would that I had stayed with the Phaeacians
right there;
sentences.i: If only I had stayed there with the Phaeacians;
sentences.n: αἴθ’ is αἴθε ‘would that’, and ὄφελον is the aorist of ὀφέλλω ‘owe, ought’, which with an infinitive makes a wish that cannot now be met: ‘I ought to have stayed’. μεῖναι is the aorist infinitive of μένω ‘stay’, and παρὰ Φαιήκεσσιν ‘beside the Phaeacians’ has the dative plural in -εσσιν. αὐτοῦ is ‘right there’, an adverb from the genitive of αὐτός. The unit begins mid-line, after the question mark, and ends at the ano teleia in line 205.

sentences.t:
ἐγὼ δέ κεν ἄλλον ὑπερμενέων βασιλήων
ἐξικόμην, ὅς κέν μ’ ἐφίλει καὶ ἔπεμπε νέεσθαι.
sentences.tr:
egō de ken allon hypermeneōn basilēōn
exikomēn, hos ken m’ ephilei kai epempe neesthai.
sentences.l:
and I to another of the exceeding-strong kings
would have come, who would have treated me as a friend and sent me to return.
sentences.i: and I would have come to some other of the kings of surpassing strength, who would have treated me as a friend and sent me on my way home.
sentences.n: δέ κεν … ἐξικόμην is ‘and I would have come’: κεν with an aorist indicative is a past potential, and ἐξικόμην is the aorist middle of ἐξικνέομαι ‘arrive at’. ἄλλον … βασιλήων is ‘another of the kings’, a partitive genitive, with βασιλήων the epic genitive plural; ὑπερμενής is ‘of surpassing strength’, from ὑπέρ and μένος ‘strength’. ὅς κέν μ’ ἐφίλει καὶ ἔπεμπε has a second κεν with two imperfects: ἐφίλει from φιλέω, ‘treat as a φίλος, with the kindness due a guest’, and ἔπεμπε ‘sent’. νέεσθαι is the epic infinitive of νέομαι ‘go, return’, and gives the purpose of the sending: ‘to return home’.

sentences.t:
νῦν δ’ οὔτ’ ἄρ πῃ θέσθαι ἐπίσταμαι, οὐδὲ μὲν αὐτοῦ
καλλείψω, μή πώς μοι ἕλωρ ἄλλοισι γένηται.
sentences.tr:
nyn d’ out’ ar pēi thesthai epistamai, oude men autou
kalleipsō, mē pōs moi helōr alloisi genētai.
sentences.l:
But now neither anywhere to put them do I know how, nor indeed here
will I leave them, lest in some way, to me, prey for others they become.
sentences.i: But now I know of nowhere to put them, nor will I leave them here, in case they somehow become prey for others, to my loss.
sentences.n: οὔτ’ … οὐδὲ μέν is loose: the first negative has no matching οὔτε and is taken up by οὐδέ ‘nor indeed’. ἐπίσταμαι takes the infinitive θέσθαι, the aorist middle infinitive of τίθημι ‘put away for oneself, store’, and πῃ is the indefinite ‘anywhere’. αὐτοῦ is ‘here, on the spot’. καλλείψω is καταλείψω with the τ assimilated to the λ, ‘abandon’. μή πώς … γένηται is ‘lest somehow … become’, with an aorist subjunctive. ἕλωρ is ‘prey, booty’, with ἄλλοισι ‘for others’, and μοι is a dative of disadvantage, ‘to my loss’.

sentences.t:
ὢ πόποι, οὐκ ἄρα πάντα νοήμονες οὐδὲ δίκαιοι
ἦσαν Φαιήκων ἡγήτορες ἠδὲ μέδοντες,
οἵ μ’ εἰς ἄλλην γαῖαν ἀπήγαγον, ἦ τέ μ’ ἔφαντο
ἄξειν εἰς Ἰθάκην εὐδείελον, οὐδ’ ἐτέλεσσαν.
sentences.tr:
ō popoi, ouk ara panta noēmones oude dikaioi
ēsan Phaiēkōn hēgētores ēde medontes,
hoi m’ eis allēn gaian apēgagon, ē te m’ ephanto
axein eis Ithakēn eudeielon, oud’ etelessan.
sentences.l:
Ah, not after all altogether discerning nor just
were the leaders and lords of the Phaeacians,
who to another land led me away, they who truly said
they would bring me to clear-seen Ithaca, and did not accomplish it.
sentences.i: Ah, so the leaders and lords of the Phaeacians were not wholly discerning or just, who led me away to another land, though they did say that they would bring me to clear-seen Ithaca, and did not accomplish it.
sentences.n: Odysseus is wrong, and the reader knows it: lines 113–121 showed the Phaeacians bringing him home and leaving him with every gift. οὐκ ἄρα πάντα is ‘not, as it turns out, altogether’: ἄρα marks a discovery, and πάντα is an adverbial accusative that softens the denial. νοήμονες ‘discerning’ is built on νόος ‘mind’. ἡγήτορες ‘leaders’ and μέδοντες ‘lords’ are the pair of line 186. οἵ … ἀπήγαγον is ‘who led away’, and ἦ τέ ‘truly’ goes with μ’ ἔφαντο ‘they said (that they would bring) me’: μ’ is με, the object of the future infinitive ἄξειν ‘would bring’, whose subject is the same as that of ἔφαντο. ἐυδείελον ‘clear-seen’ is the epithet of Ithaca; the ancient explanations conflict, from δείελος ‘evening’ or from δῆλος ‘visible’. ἐτέλεσσαν is the aorist of τελέω with doubled σσ, the verb of τελεῖται at 178.

sentences.t:
Ζεὺς σφέας τίσαιτο ἱκετήσιος, ὅς τε καὶ ἄλλους
ἀνθρώπους ἐφορᾷ καὶ τίνυται ὅς τις ἁμάρτῃ.
sentences.tr:
Zeus spheas tisaito hiketēsios, hos te kai allous
anthrōpous ephorāi kai tinytai hos tis hamartēi.
sentences.l:
Zeus of suppliants may take vengeance on them, who also other
men oversees and takes vengeance on whoever errs.
sentences.i: May Zeus, the god of suppliants, take vengeance on them, he who watches over other men as well and takes vengeance on whoever does wrong.
sentences.n: ἱκετήσιος ‘of suppliants’ is a title of Zeus as protector of the ἱκέτης ‘suppliant’; Odysseus thinks of himself as wronged by those who should have kept their word. τίσαιτο is the aorist optative middle of τίνυμαι ‘take vengeance on, punish’, a wish, with σφέας ‘them’ (σφεῖς) as its object. ὅς τε … ἐφορᾷ is ‘who, as one does, watches over’: the τε marks a general truth about the god, and ἐφορᾷ is the contracted ἐφοράει ‘oversees’. τίνυται is the present of the same verb as τίσαιτο. ὅς τις ἁμάρτῃ is ‘whoever errs’, the aorist subjunctive of ἁμαρτάνω. As transmitted, line 213 is metrically irregular at τίσαιτο, whose short final syllable has to count as long at the main caesura, and σφέας is read as one syllable, as usual in Homer.

sentences.t:
ἀλλ’ ἄγε δὴ τὰ χρήματ’ ἀριθμήσω καὶ ἴδωμαι,
μή τί μοι οἴχωνται κοίλης ἐπὶ νηὸς ἄγοντες.
sentences.tr:
all’ age dē ta chrēmat’ arithmēsō kai idōmai,
mē ti moi oichōntai koilēs epi nēos agontes.
sentences.l:
But come now, the goods let me count and look,
lest anything of mine they have gone off with, on a hollow ship carrying.”
sentences.i: But come now, let me count up the goods and look, in case they have gone off with something of mine, carrying it away in their hollow ship.”
sentences.n: ἀλλ’ ἄγε δή is ‘but come now’, an exhortation to himself, and ἀριθμήσω (a short-vowel subjunctive, though it could be read as a future) and ἴδωμαι (an aorist subjunctive) are first-person forms, ‘let me count and see’. μή τί … οἴχωνται is ‘lest … they have gone’: οἴχομαι ‘be gone’ has a perfect sense, here in the subjunctive after μή of fear. ἄγοντες ‘carrying off’ completes it, ‘gone off carrying’, and μοι ‘of mine’ is a dative of disadvantage. κοίλης ἐπὶ νηός is ‘on a hollow ship’, the genitive after ἐπί meaning ‘on board’.
